newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan govt slammed for endorsing strike.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan govt slammed for endorsing strike.

text.p: Venezuelan business leaders poured scorn on the government on Tuesday for endorsing the country's first national strike in eight years.
Wednesday's 12-hour stoppage, called by the Venezuelan Workers Confederation (CTV), the country's largest union, is aimed at putting pressure on private sector companies to raise salaries.
It threatened to ruin a fragile consensus for a tough economic programme that President Rafael Caldera's administration reluctantly implemented last year.

Union and government officials have rounded on business leaders for failing to meet a commitment to raise salaries made in March in a ground-breaking agreement to reform the complex social security system.

Francisco Natera, head of business chamber Fedecamaras, labeled the strike "a smokescreen aimed at covering up the government's inability to tackle inflation, fiscal laxity and the constant deterioration of real salaries."
According to official figures, high inflation and tardy wage rises have cut real wages to one-third of their 1960s level.
Government ministers have said the strike is justified and encouraged public sector employees to join the walkout, leading national daily El Nacional on Tuesday to dub it "the official strike".
"Of course there is labour unrest...that's why there will be a strike tomorrow," Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said.
The strike was also called to protest last week's 27 percent hike in gasoline prices. It brought the average price for a litre of fuel to 70 bolivars ($0.14) -- still among the cheapest in the world.
With its membership concentrated in the public sector, it was not clear how much support the CTV would get for the walkout.
Bus and metro workers have said they will join the strike, guaranteeing traffic chaos in major cities, in particular the capital Caracas.

State oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), which controls the largest oil reserves outside the Middle East, said white collar staff would stand in for striking workers, ensuring that pumps and refineries would run smoothly.
Telephone and electricity services were expected to operate normally and airports would remain open, officials said.
Business leaders insisted the government should provide special transport to ensure that workers unwilling to join could get to work.
Defence Minister Tito Rincon said the government did not expect the strike to spark off violent protests but that troops were on alert nonetheless.
